theme: AI at Work: Start Where You Are
title: Your First Win
titleHtml: Your first AI win is one chore away.
tagline: Hands-on: one safe AI use case for your daily work.
description: A 45-minute hands-on virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: pick one safe chore from your own week, write a plain-English ask, and check the result before you use it. No AI experience needed.
heroLead: This hour assumes you have never opened an AI tool. Bring one chore from your regular week; you will learn the traffic light that keeps it safe, ask for help in plain English, and check the result like an editor. That is a complete first win.
objectives: Pick one green-light chore from your own week that AI can safely draft
Write a plain-English ask that gives the tool the job, the details, and the shape you want
Check the result for accuracy and voice before anything leaves your hands
missionTie: The great university of the 21st Century gets built in ordinary workweeks. Every staff member who hands a chore to AI safely puts an hour back into work that needs a human, and Exceptional Core Operations grows by exactly that much.
goalLead: Goal 3 measures a workforce that is ready for AI, and readiness starts with one real use each. Today you run yours: one chore, one ask, one check.

agenda.d: The traffic light, and finding one green-light task in your own week.
Plain English works: the job, the details, and the shape you want back.
You are the editor. What to verify before the draft goes anywhere.

manifesto: Start where you are: one chore, one ask, one check.

sections.headline: Your week is full of green lights.
sections.lead: AI is at its best on chores: first drafts, tidy summaries, notes turned into clean sentences. The traffic light decides what is safe. Green, public or generic: go. Yellow, internal work: approved VU tools only. Red, private information about people: never.
sections.group: In pairs: each name one chore from your own week and call its light. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one chore from your own week and call its light: green, yellow, or red.

interaction.intro: Every use case starts with this call. Read each chore and pick its light.
interaction.passMsg: You can call the light. Green chores are your starting lane; yellow waits for approved VU tools; red stays out, every time.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The light follows the information in the chore: public or generic is green, internal work is yellow inside approved VU tools, and private information about people is always red.

items.q: Drafting a friendly reminder about a campus event that is already on the public calendar.
items.why: Public event, generic wording. A perfect first win: the tool drafts in seconds, and you polish the details you know.

items.q: Summarizing notes from an internal team meeting so you can share highlights with the group.
items.why: Internal content is yellow: fine inside approved VU tools, off limits in anything else. The chore is great; the venue matters.

items.q: Writing a sensitive email about a student's health situation, with the details pasted in.
items.why: Private information about a person is red, always. AI can suggest a generic structure for hard emails; the specifics never go in.

sections.headline: Ask like you would ask a colleague.
sections.lead: There is a myth that talking to AI takes special training. Plain English works. Tell the tool the job, give it the details that matter, and say what shape you want back. The same sentences you would use to brief a helpful colleague are the ones that work here.
sections.group: In pairs: say the plain-English ask for the chore you named in section one. Does your partner know exactly what you want back? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write the plain-English ask for the chore you named in section one: the job, the details, the shape.

interaction.intro: Your chore: a first draft of a thank-you note to volunteers after a public campus event. Choose what you tell the tool.

opts.coach: The tool can only work with what you said. A vague job gets a vague draft that could be about anyone, anywhere.

opts.t: Write a thank-you note to our event volunteers.
opts.coach: Clear job, thin details. The draft will be usable and generic; you will spend your time adding everything that made the event yours.

opts.t: Write a warm, short thank-you to the 20 volunteers who ran Saturday's campus book fair.
opts.coach: Job, tone, length, and the details that matter, in one plain sentence. Specific asks come back sounding close to done.

opts.t: Say nothing and take whatever comes back.
opts.coach: The tool will guess: maybe three paragraphs, maybe a formal letter. Every guess it makes is an edit you make later.
Length is a good start. Adding the format and the sign-off you want saves another round of fixes.

opts.t: One short paragraph, warm tone, ending with an invite to next spring's fair.
opts.coach: Now the tool knows exactly what done looks like. Describing the shape you want is the easiest skill in this whole hour.

heads.strong: A draft you would nearly send. Two small edits and it sounds like you on a good day.
heads.mid: A usable draft with generic bones. Ten minutes of editing, which still beats a blank page.
heads.weak: A draft about nobody in particular. You will rewrite most of it, and the tool takes the blame for a thin ask.

reactions.strong: You send the note twenty minutes after the event wrap-up instead of next Thursday. Two volunteers reply that it was the nicest thank-you they have gotten, and the hour you saved went to work that needed you.
reactions.mid: The note goes out a day later after real editing. Next time you add the details up front and discover the editing almost disappears.
reactions.weak: The draft sits in your folder because fixing it feels like starting over. The lesson is cheap: the tool answers the ask it was given.

sections.headline: You are the editor.
sections.lead: AI drafts with total confidence and zero guarantee. Sometimes it invents a detail, gets a name wrong, or strikes a tone you would never use. The rule that keeps you safe is simple: the draft ships after you have read every line and can stand behind every fact.
sections.group: In pairs: tell each other about a time a confident-sounding document turned out to be wrong. What would have caught it? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Recall a time a confident-sounding document turned out to be wrong. What would have caught it?

card.text: Before an AI draft goes anywhere, check facts (every name, date, and number), fit (is this what you meant to say?), and voice (does it sound like you?). If you cannot verify a detail, cut it or confirm it yourself.

interaction.q: The tool's draft includes a detail you did not provide and cannot verify. What do you do?

opts.t: Keep it; the tool probably knows
opts.why: The tool writes what sounds likely, and likely-sounding details are sometimes wrong. Anything you cannot verify has no place in your work.

opts.t: Cut it or confirm it yourself before the draft moves
opts.why: Exactly. You are the editor, and your name goes on the result. Verified details stay; everything else goes.

opts.t: Send it with a note that AI wrote it
opts.why: A disclaimer hands the checking to your reader. The check is your job, and it takes two minutes on a chore-sized draft.

recap.q: Which chore is a green light for your first AI use?
opts: Summarizing an internal meeting in a free tool
Drafting a note about a public campus event
An email with details about a person's health
Anything, as long as you check the result
recap.why: The light follows the information. Public or generic goes; internal waits for approved VU tools; private information about people never goes in.

recap.q: What belongs in a good plain-English ask?
opts: The job, the details that matter, and the shape you want
A request to make it sound impressive
recap.why: The same brief you would give a helpful colleague. Specific asks come back close to done; vague asks come back vague.

recap.q: What must happen before an AI draft leaves your hands?
opts: Nothing, if the chore was green
A colleague signs off on it
You verify every fact and make it sound like you
You add a note saying AI helped
recap.why: The green light covers what goes in; the editor's rule covers what comes out. Facts verified, voice yours, then it ships.

recapMsgs.high: You have the whole loop: chore, ask, check. Go run it on your real week.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Reread the editor's rule, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One chore. One ask. One check.
capstone.lead: Pick the chore from your own week and the moment you will run it. Nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: The green-light chore, and the ask you will make in plain English.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. draft the newsletter blurb about the public lecture series
capstone.practiceLabel: Which first win do you run?

practices.name: The first draft
practices.move: Hand the tool one green-light writing chore with a specific ask, then edit the draft into your own voice.

practices.name: The tidy-up
practices.move: Give the tool your rough notes on something public or generic and ask for clean, short sentences.

practices.name: The plain explainer
practices.move: Ask the tool to explain a public topic you need to understand, then verify the pieces you plan to use.

whens.out: The first win happens today, while the ask is still fresh in your head.
The first win happens this week, tied to a real deadline already on your list.
The first win happens at the navigator-led First-AI-Win sandbox session, with help in the room.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did the check catch, and what did the saved time free you to do?

closing.headline: One chore down. A habit begun.
closing.lead: You called the light, wrote the ask, and learned the editor's rule. Thursday's Thrive Thursday builds the adaptability that keeps you steady while tools like this keep changing.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Run the chore on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it exactly as built: the ask, the check, and one line about what the check caught. If you would rather try with company, the navigator-led First-AI-Win sandbox session is open to everyone this month.
closing.brandline: Start where you are. Check before it ships.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; many attendees will be opening an AI tool for the first time. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites and zero jargon; December is the AI at Work month.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did you run the chore on your card? What did the check catch? What chore gets the next green light?' Count of completed first wins is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: Pick the chore
s1.purpose: Install the traffic light and have every learner find one green-light chore in their own week.
s1.say: If you have never opened an AI tool, you are exactly who this hour was built for. One rule keeps everything safe, and it fits on a sticky note. Green, public or generic information: go. Yellow, internal work: approved VU tools only. Red, private information about people: never. Everything we do today lives in green.
facilitate: Run Call the light live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the red case, pause: the chore was kind, and the information still made it red.
Run the breakout: one chore from your own week, call its light.

ask.q: What green-light chore from your own week came to mind first?
ask.respond: All perfect. Chore-sized is the point: your first win should be small enough to finish today and check in two minutes.

s1.debrief: The light follows the information, and green is a big lane. Most weeks hold more green chores than anyone expects.
s1.watchFor: People whose whole week feels yellow or red. Point them at the generic side of their job: announcements, outlines, and public material are green even in sensitive roles.
s1.transition: You have the chore. Now the ask, in plain English.
s1.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one chore from chat.

s2.title: Write the ask
s2.purpose: Prove that plain English works: the job, the details that matter, and the shape you want back.
s2.say: Here is the best news of the month: talking to an AI tool takes no special language. You brief it the way you would brief a helpful colleague. Here is the job, here are the details that matter, here is the shape I want back. The clearer the ask, the closer the draft comes back to done. Let's build one together.
facilitate: Run Build the ask; two minutes to make both choices and send it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: a specific job plus a described shape equals a draft worth keeping.

ask.q: What detail would you add to make the volunteer thank-you ask even better?
expect: A specific moment from the event
The audience it is going to
ask.respond: All good adds. Details you provide are details you already trust, which also makes the check at the end faster.

s2.debrief: The tool answers the ask it was given. Plain English, real details, described shape: that is the whole craft.
s2.watchFor: People apologizing for weak first asks. Normalize it fast: everyone's first ask is thin, and one more honest sentence usually fixes it.
s2.transition: The draft is back. Before it goes anywhere, you become the editor.
s2.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

s3.title: Check before you use
s3.purpose: Install the editor's rule: verify facts, fit, and voice before any draft leaves your hands.
s3.say: One honest warning and you are ready. The tool writes with total confidence whether it is right or wrong. Sometimes it invents a detail or misses your meaning, so the last step of every use is the check: every fact verified, the message actually yours, the voice actually you. Two minutes of editing keeps your name safe on everything you send.
facilitate: Read the editor's rule card aloud, once, slowly.
Run the knowledge check; ask which answer people picked before revealing.
Run the breakout on the confident-sounding document that turned out wrong.

ask.q: Why does the check stay your job even when the draft looks perfect?
expect: The tool cannot know what is true in my world
Polish is exactly when errors slip through
ask.respond: Right on all counts. The polish is the trap; read every line like an editor, especially the impressive ones.

s3.debrief: Facts, fit, voice. If you cannot verify a detail, cut it or confirm it yourself. Then it ships.
s3.watchFor: Learners concluding AI is too risky to touch at all. Rebalance: the check takes two minutes on a chore-sized draft, and the chore used to take an hour.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your first-win card.
s3.coreNote: Core: read the card, run the check, skip the breakout.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One green-light chore from your own week, the plain-English ask you will make, and the moment you will run it. If you would rather try with help nearby, pick the sandbox session as your moment. Build the card and copy it somewhere you will see it. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with the whole loop: one chore, one ask, one check. Run it this week and tell your team what the check caught. Thursday's Thrive Thursday takes on the other half of new tools: adaptability, staying steady while things keep changing. And if you want company for your first run, the navigators are hosting a First-AI-Win sandbox session this month; the LinkedIn Learning course Generative AI for Business Leaders pairs well once your first win is behind you.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A learner starts describing real internal or personal content they want to paste into a tool
contingencies.then: Redirect gently and publicly: 'Keep it green for today: public or generic only.' Praise the instinct to try, then point the yellow work at approved VU tools.

contingencies.if: Someone says they are too far behind to ever catch up with AI
contingencies.then: Slow the room down: this session assumes zero experience on purpose. One chore, one ask, one check is the entire skill today, and the sandbox session exists for exactly this feeling.

toughQuestions.q: Which tool should I actually use?
toughQuestions.a: For green-light chores, any of the approved tools listed on the Anchor's Edge dashboard work, and your navigator can point you to the current list. The habit transfers: the light, the plain-English ask, and the check work the same everywhere, so the skill you built today is portable.

toughQuestions.q: Is using AI for my work cheating?
toughQuestions.a: Handing a chore to a tool and checking the result is the same judgment you already use with a template or a spell-checker, scaled up. The thinking, the facts, and the final call stay yours. What would cross a line is sending anything you have never read and verified yourself.

toughQuestions.q: What if the tool gives me a wrong answer and I miss it?
toughQuestions.a: That is why the first win is chore-sized: small drafts are checkable in two minutes. Verify names, dates, and numbers against sources you trust, and cut anything you cannot confirm. The editor's eye gets faster with practice; start small and it grows with you.
